nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the impressionist novel, the war tetralogy and the modern editor's craft
literary_identity: Novelist, editor and critic; the author of The Good Soldier and Parade's End, the editor of the English Review and the transatlantic review, and the great teacher of the modern novel.
biography: Born Ford Hermann Hueffer at Merton, Surrey, on 17 December 1873, the son of a German-born music critic and the grandson of the Pre-Raphaelite painter Ford Madox Brown; he published his first book at eighteen, collaborated with Conrad on The Inheritors (1901) and Romance (1903), edited the English Review (1908–09) — discovering and publishing Hardy, James, Wells, Pound and Lawrence — and the transatlantic review (1924). The Good Soldier appeared in 1915, the Parade's End tetralogy in 1924–28. He changed his surname to Ford in 1919, taught at Olivet College, Michigan, in the 1930s, and died at Deauville on 26 June 1939.
literary_profile: Ford is the great teacher of the modern novel: The Good Soldier is the most perfect English novel of the period — a study of deception told by a narrator who is himself deceived — and Parade's End is the finest English novel of the First World War and the transition from Edwardian to modern England. As editor of the English Review and the transatlantic review he published the modern movement into existence, and his criticism (The March of Literature, 1938) taught a whole generation how to read.
stylistic_characteristics: The impressionist method: the scene rendered as it strikes a mind, in broken chronology, with the narrator's hesitations left in; the deliberate withholding of information ('this is the saddest story I have ever heard'); the long, loose, conversational sentence; the progression d'effet; the editorial preface as criticism.
intellectual_concerns: Marriage, adultery and the conventions that conceal them; the Edwardian ruling class and its code; the First World War and the end of the old England; the Catholic conscience and the protestant mind; the artist and the patron; time and the reconstruction of memory.
historical_significance: Ford wrote the finest English novel of the period in The Good Soldier and the finest English war novel in Parade's End, and as editor of the English Review and the transatlantic review he made modernism publishable. He is the period's great theorist and practitioner of the impressionist novel.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: New Zealand-British; the modernist short story and the epiphany of the ordinary
literary_identity: Short-story writer; the finest English-language short-story writer of the period, the inventor of the modern story of the moment, and the central woman writer of English modernism after Woolf.
biography: Born Kathleen Mansfield Beauchamp in Wellington, New Zealand, on 14 October 1888 into a wealthy colonial family; she came to London in 1903, returned to New Zealand in 1906, and left for good in 1908. She married George Bowden (1909), met John Middleton Murry (1911), published In a German Pension (1911) and, after her brother Leslie's death in the war, the stories of Prelude (1918), Bliss (1920) and The Garden Party (1922). Tuberculosis was diagnosed in 1917; she died at Fontainebleau on 9 January 1923, aged thirty-four.
literary_profile: Mansfield made the modern short story: 'Prelude', 'The Daughters of the Late Colonel', 'At the Bay', 'The Garden Party' and 'The Fly' gave English prose a new compression and a new way of rendering the moment of perception. Her stories dissolve plot into the texture of ordinary life, and her use of the shifting point of view and the withheld conclusion is the model for the twentieth-century story. She is, with Woolf and Richardson, the central woman modernist of English prose.
stylistic_characteristics: The story without a plot: a moment of perception, a family scene, a shift of light; the multiple point of view and the free indirect style; the exact rendering of a child's or a servant's consciousness; the detail that carries the emotion; the ending that simply closes.
intellectual_concerns: Childhood, the family and the New Zealand of her memory; the woman's life, marriage and solitude; illness, the sanatorium and death; the servant and the class below stairs; the ordinary moment and its hidden violence; exile and the lost home.
historical_significance: Mansfield is the greatest English-language short-story writer of the period and the central innovator of the modern story: 'Prelude', 'At the Bay' and 'The Garden Party' changed what a short story could do, her technique of the epiphany influenced every subsequent practitioner, and her letters and journals are among the finest autobiographical writing of the century.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; the synthetic Scots lyric and the modernist long poem of national self-examination
literary_identity: Poet and polemicist; the founder of the Scottish Renaissance, the author of A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle, and the most important Scottish poet of the century.
biography: Born Christopher Murray Grieve at Langholm, Dumfriesshire, on 11 August 1892, the son of a postman; he trained as a teacher, worked as a journalist in Montrose, founded the Scottish Chapbook (1922) and the Scottish Nation, and published Sangschaw (1925), Penny Wheep (1926) and A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle (1926) under the name Hugh MacDiarmid. He joined the Communist Party (1934), was expelled and rejoined, published the long poems To Circumjack Cencrastus (1930), In Memoriam James Joyce (1955) and The Kind of Poetry I Want (1961), and died in Edinburgh on 9 September 1978.
literary_profile: MacDiarmid founded the modern literature of Scotland: A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle is the century's greatest long poem in Scots and one of the great poems of national self-examination in any language, and his synthetic Scots — made from Jamieson's dictionary and the ballads — gave the language a modern poetic instrument. His later English long poems extended the same ambition into science, linguistics and world culture.
stylistic_characteristics: The synthetic Scots lyric with its dictionary richness; the long poem built of lyric bursts and argument; the sudden shift from Scots to English and back; the manifesto, the pamphlet and the insult; the scientific and linguistic vocabulary carried into verse.
intellectual_concerns: Scotland, the Scots language and its loss; Calvinism and the Scottish psyche; the industrial city and the emptied glen; communism and the political poem; language itself as a national inheritance; the poet as a public scourge.
historical_significance: MacDiarmid is the central Scottish poet of the century and the founder of the Scottish Renaissance: A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle is a permanent long poem, his synthetic Scots restored the language as a poetic medium, and his polemics made Scottish literature a modern question. He is the period's great poet of national identity.

birthplace: Hillhead of Segget, Auchterless, Aberdeenshire, Scotland
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; the agrarian novel of the Mearns and the Scots prose of the modern novel
literary_identity: Novelist; the author of Sunset Song and A Scots Quair, the finest Scottish novel of the century and the greatest English-language novel of rural dispossession.
biography: Born James Leslie Mitchell at Hillhead of Segget, Aberdeenshire, on 13 February 1901; his family moved to the farming country of the Mearns, which became the 'Kinraddie' of his fiction. He left school at fourteen, worked as a journalist in Aberdeen, Glasgow and London, served in the Royal Army Service Corps in the Middle East, and wrote under the name Lewis Grassic Gibbon: Sunset Song (1932), Cloud Howe (1933) and Grey Granite (1934), collected as A Scots Quair, together with the historical and anthropological books of his last years. He died in Welwyn Garden City on 7 February 1935, aged thirty-three.
literary_profile: Gibbon wrote the greatest Scottish novel of the century: Sunset Song is the elegy of the crofting world destroyed by the war and the machine, and A Scots Quair is the most complete account in fiction of Scotland's passage from the land to the city in a single generation. His prose — a Scots-inflected English that moves between the parish voice and the modern narrative — is one of the period's great inventions.
stylistic_characteristics: The Scots-inflected English narrative that shifts register with the characters' consciousness; the choric parish voice at the chapter's opening; the lyric description of landscape and weather; the historical sweep of a community rather than a life; the direct address of the tale-teller.
intellectual_concerns: The land, the croft and the vanishing rural Scotland; the First World War and its destruction of the parish; the industrial city and the class struggle; Calvinism and the Scottish mind; the woman's passage through three worlds (Chris Guthrie); progress and its cost.
historical_significance: Gibbon wrote the finest Scottish novel of the period and one of the great novels of rural dispossession in English: Sunset Song and A Scots Quair record the destruction of a whole way of life with lyric power, and his Scots prose gave the modern Scottish novel its language. He is the prose counterpart of MacDiarmid in the Scottish Renaissance.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; the mythic lyric and the autobiography of lost Eden
literary_identity: Poet, critic and translator; the great Orcadian lyric poet of the century and the author of The Story and the Fable, one of the finest Scottish autobiographies.
biography: Born Edwin Muir on a farm at Deerness, Orkney, on 15 May 1887; the family moved to Glasgow in 1901 and was destroyed by the city's poverty, an experience that became the ground of all his poetry. He worked as a clerk in a bone factory and an office, married Willa Anderson in 1919, translated Kafka with her, wrote criticism for The Freeman, the New Age and The Listener, and published First Poems (1925), The Narrow Place (1943), The Voyage (1946) and One Foot in Eden (1956). He died at Swaffham Prior, Cambridgeshire, on 3 January 1959.
literary_profile: Muir is the great Scottish poet of the modern lyric: his poems of Eden, the fall, the journey and the lost childhood are among the finest in twentieth-century English, and The Story and the Fable (1940) is one of the great autobiographies of the period. With his wife Willa he translated Kafka's novels into English for the first time, an act of transmission as important as his own verse.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain, mythic, unnervingly simple lyric; the dream image held in regular stanza; the archetype deployed without ornament; the child's vision and the adult's guilt; the prose of an autobiography that reads like a fable.
intellectual_concerns: Eden, the fall and the lost childhood; the city and the destruction of the family; the journey, the voyage and the dream; Scotland, Orkney and the inheritance of myth; time, dream and the archetypal image; the poet's vocation.
historical_significance: Muir is the finest Scottish lyric poet of the period and one of the great autobiographers: his mythic poems of Eden and the journey are permanent, The Story and the Fable is a central Scottish autobiography, and his translations of Kafka gave English the writer who remade the modern novel.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the experimental prose, the portrait and the syntax of repetition
literary_identity: Writer and patron; the great American experimentalist of the period, the host of the Paris salon that made the Lost Generation, and the inventor of a prose without nouns.
biography: Born Gertrude Stein in Allegheny, Pennsylvania, on 3 February 1874 into a wealthy German-Jewish family; she studied at Radcliffe under William James and at Johns Hopkins medicine, moved to Paris in 1903 with her brother Leo, and began collecting the paintings that made 27 rue de Fleurus the centre of modern art. Three Lives appeared in 1909, Tender Buttons in 1914, The Making of Americans in 1925 and The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas in 1933. She lived with Alice B. Toklas from 1907 and died at Neuilly-sur-Seine on 27 July 1946.
literary_profile: Stein is the great experimentalist of the period: her 'continuous present', her repetition, her abolition of the noun and her cubist portraits made a prose that dismantles the conventions of English syntax, and she taught a generation of American writers — Hemingway among them — how to write a sentence. The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas is one of the period's most entertaining books, and her Paris salon was the social centre of modernism.
stylistic_characteristics: The continuous present and the deliberate repetition; the abolition of the noun and the article; the portrait made of repeated traits; the cubist arrangement of phrases; the plain declarative sentence used against its own grammar; the memoir written as a joke and a history at once.
intellectual_concerns: The making of Americans and the American family; the ordinary object and the ordinary life; the Paris of the avant-garde; genius, patronage and the woman artist; the war and the occupation; language itself as a subject.
historical_significance: Stein is the central American experimental writer of the period: Three Lives and Tender Buttons changed the possibilities of English prose, her Paris salon made modernism a social fact, The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas is a permanent memoir, and her influence on Hemingway, Anderson and the American sentence is beyond calculation.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the small-town story and the American grotesque
literary_identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the author of Winesburg, Ohio, the book that gave American fiction its modern small-town story and its term for the inarticulate outsider.
biography: Born Sherwood Anderson in Camden, Ohio, on 13 September 1876; he left school at fourteen, served in the Spanish-American War, ran a paint factory in Elyria, Ohio, and in 1912 walked out of it in a nervous collapse to become a writer. Windy McPherson's Son (1916) and Marching Men (1917) preceded Winesburg, Ohio (1919), which made his name; he published many novels and stories, edited two little magazines, and died in Panama on 8 March 1941.
literary_profile: Anderson wrote the book that made the modern American short story possible: Winesburg, Ohio gave American fiction the small town as a place of hidden loneliness — the 'grotesques' whose truth is not told — and its influence runs through Hemingway, Faulkner, Wolfe and Carver. He was the first American writer to make the inarticulate the subject of the form.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain, bare, repetitive sentence; the story without plot, built on a single moment of longing; the recurring town and the recurring characters; the framed sequence of stories as a novel; the voice of a man who cannot say what he means.
intellectual_concerns: The small town and its hidden lives; loneliness and the failure of speech; sex, adolescence and the fear of the body; the industrial town against the old agrarian America; the artist and the escape from the town; the grotesque and the truth of the outsider.
historical_significance: Anderson wrote the founding book of the modern American short story: Winesburg, Ohio changed what an American story could be about, gave American fiction the small town as a place of hidden lives, and was acknowledged by Hemingway, Faulkner and Wolfe as the source of their generation's prose.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the blues poem, the Harlem Renaissance lyric and the satire of the colour line
literary_identity: Poet, novelist, playwright and columnist; the central poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the first American to make the blues a literary form, and the most widely read Black writer of the century.
biography: Born James Mercer Langston Hughes in Joplin, Missouri, on 1 February 1902; he was raised by his grandmother in Lawrence, Kansas, and his mother in Illinois and Ohio, spent a year at Columbia, worked as a ship's cook and a busboy, and was 'discovered' in a Washington restaurant by Vachel Lindsay in 1925. The Weary Blues appeared in 1926 and Fine Clothes to the Jew in 1927; he wrote the novel Not Without Laughter (1930), the play Mulatto (1935), the Jesse B. Semple stories and the Montage of a Dream Deferred (1951). He died in New York on 22 May 1967.
literary_profile: Hughes is the central poet of the Harlem Renaissance and the first American poet to make the blues and jazz a literary form: The Weary Blues put the blues on the printed page, 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers', 'I, Too' and 'Harlem' are among the most quoted American poems, and his Jesse B. Semple columns made a Black vernacular voice a national institution. He wrote for the whole race, not for the salon, and that is the source of his permanence.
stylistic_characteristics: The blues stanza and the jazz line; the plain vernacular speech of Harlem; the repetition-with-variation of the blues form; the short ironic lyric with a withheld pain; the comic monologue (Simple); the poem that asks a question instead of making a statement.
intellectual_concerns: Race, the colour line and the New Negro; Harlem and the Great Migration; the blues, jazz and the pleasure economy; the dream deferred and the American promise; the working Black man and the comic survivor (Semple); Africa, the South and the ancestral past.
historical_significance: Hughes is the central African American poet of the century and the founding figure of the Harlem Renaissance in verse: he made the blues a literary form, wrote the period's most quoted poems of Black America, created the Jesse B. Semple voice, and maintained a public Black poetry for four decades when almost no one else did.
